schema.description: {{COMPANY_NAME}} reusable Merlino Catalogue threat-profile template for System Integrator / MSP organisations. TP-05 models Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise across developer identities, repositories, CI/CD pipelines, hosted/self-hosted runners, package and dependency ecosystems, artifact registries, secrets, service connections, signing/authentication material and software release/distribution. It incorporates current MITRE ATT&CK v19.2 threat context for TeamPCP, Shai-Hulud, Mini Shai-Hulud, TeamPCP Cloud Stealer and ShinyHunters, while remaining a reusable generic profile rather than an actor-specific one. The organisation name is represented by {{COMPANY_NAME}} for rapid reuse. Records are Pick=true because every row is intentionally included in the candidate TP-05 profile.

data.Name: TP-05 | Search Open Websites/Domains: Code Repositories
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search public or exposed code repositories for credentials, API keys, internal URLs, pipeline definitions, package metadata, developer identities, infrastructure configuration and software weaknesses. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Public repositories are a direct intelligence source for attackers targeting system integrators. They may reveal how software is built, which CI/CD platforms are used, who maintains packages, and whether secrets or customer-specific configuration are exposed. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Public GitHub/GitLab/Azure DevOps repositories, Source code, Pipeline YAML, Developer identities, Configuration files. Attack-path stage: Locate Public Development Assets. Detection opportunities: External repository secret scanning; Code exposure monitoring; Alert on accidental public repository creation; Monitor public forks of internal projects. Defensive considerations: Private-by-default repositories; Secret scanning; Repository classification; Prevent public conversion for sensitive repos; Remove customer secrets from code.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Public repositories are a direct intelligence source for attackers targeting system integrators. They may reveal how software is built, which CI/CD platforms are used, who maintains packages, and whether secrets or customer-specific configuration are exposed. Threat-led context: ShinyHunters is documented by MITRE as searching target GitHub repositories for credentials/API keys and source-code weaknesses. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Reconnaissance; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Acquire credentials associated with developers, repository administrators, DevOps engineers, package maintainers and build-system operators. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer and DevOps identities often hold access to repositories, CI/CD secrets, artifact registries, cloud deployments and customer projects. Their compromise can bridge identity compromise directly into software supply-chain control. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Git identities, Azure DevOps users, GitHub/GitLab accounts, DevOps administrators, Package maintainers. Attack-path stage: Target Developer Credentials. Detection opportunities: Credential exposure monitoring; Identity Protection; Monitor developer credentials in public leaks and repositories. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Dedicated admin identities; Credential hygiene; No shared developer accounts.

Defensive considerations: Minimise unnecessary publication of privileged software-delivery roles; Use approval separation.

data.Name: TP-05 | Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Identify who controls repositories, package registries, CI/CD infrastructure, service connections, signing keys and releases. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: In decentralised development organisations, each business unit may use different platforms and processes. Attackers benefit from discovering exactly which teams have weak or highly privileged delivery paths. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Map Software Delivery Responsibilities. Primary assets at risk: DevOps administrators, Repository owners, Release managers, Cloud deployment owners, Signing-key custodians. Attack-path stage: Map Software Delivery Responsibilities. Detection opportunities: Threat-intelligence monitoring around named technical roles; Review public org/repository role exposure. Defensive considerations: Document ownership centrally; Separate duties between commit, approval and release; Maintain privileged-role inventory.

Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Least privilege; Repository role governance; PIM/JIT where supported.

data.Name: TP-05 | Steal Application Access Token
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Steal GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, npm, package-registry, OIDC, OAuth, CI/CD runner or cloud access tokens. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: CI/CD ecosystems depend heavily on short-lived and long-lived tokens. A stolen token may be sufficient to clone private code, modify workflows, publish packages, access cloud deployments or create new repositories without the user's password. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Credential Access. Primary assets at risk: GITHUB_TOKEN, GitHub PAT, Azure DevOps PAT, OIDC tokens, npm tokens, Cloud deployment tokens, CI/CD runner tokens. Attack-path stage: Steal CI/CD and Repository Tokens. Detection opportunities: Token use from unusual runner/account/IP; New token creation; Repository API activity outside normal pipeline context; Unexpected package publishing. Defensive considerations: Short-lived tokens; OIDC/workload federation; Fine-grained PATs; Token scoping; Immediate token rotation after compromise.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: CI/CD ecosystems depend heavily on short-lived and long-lived tokens. A stolen token may be sufficient to clone private code, modify workflows, publish packages, access cloud deployments or create new repositories without the user's password. Threat-led context: TeamPCP Cloud Stealer and Mini Shai-Hulud are documented stealing CI/CD tokens; ShinyHunters has stolen OAuth credentials from DevOps personnel/repositories. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Credential Access; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Description: Use stolen application or access tokens to authenticate to repositories, package registries, cloud services or CI/CD APIs. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Token reuse allows an attacker to move from one compromised component to another: for example from a developer identity to GitHub, from GitHub Actions to cloud resources, or from a package registry to additional maintained packages. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Lateral Movement. Primary assets at risk: Repository APIs, CI/CD APIs, Package registries, Cloud APIs, Artifact stores. Attack-path stage: Reuse Stolen CI/CD Token. Detection opportunities: API use from abnormal client/location; Token used outside expected pipeline; Token used to enumerate/publish multiple projects. Defensive considerations: Fine-grained permissions; Short-lived tokens; Workload identity federation; Revoke on suspicious use.

data.Name: TP-05 | Exploit Public-Facing Application
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Exploit an internet-facing self-hosted source-control, CI/CD, artifact repository, issue tracker or development service. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Where system integrators expose self-hosted GitLab, Jenkins, TeamCity, artifact registries or related services, a vulnerability can bypass identity-focused controls and provide direct access to the software delivery environment. Applicability: Self-Hosted / Public DevOps Conditional. Software supply-chain stage: Exploit DevOps / Developer Platform. Primary assets at risk: Jenkins, GitLab, TeamCity, Artifact registries, Developer portals. Attack-path stage: Exploit DevOps / Developer Platform. Detection opportunities: WAF/IDS exploit signals; Application audit anomalies; Unexpected administrative sessions after exploitation. Defensive considerations: Rapid patching; Internet exposure reduction; WAF; MFA; Network isolation of CI/CD admin surfaces.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Where system integrators expose self-hosted GitLab, Jenkins, TeamCity, artifact registries or related services, a vulnerability can bypass identity-focused controls and provide direct access to the software delivery environment. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Self-Hosted / Public DevOps Conditional; SupplyChainStage=Exploit DevOps / Developer Platform; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Description: Use VPN or other external remote administration services with compromised developer or DevOps credentials to access self-hosted runners, build hosts or development networks. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Self-hosted CI/CD infrastructure may reside inside trusted networks. Attack-path stage: Access Developer / Build Infrastructure. Detection opportunities: New source/device for developer VPN; Remote access outside expected development windows. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named accounts; Network segmentation; Restrict remote access to build systems.

data.Name: TP-05 | Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search and collect source code, commit history, pipeline definitions, secrets, tokens, customer configuration and architecture information from code repositories. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Code repositories are crown-jewel information stores for system integrators. They can reveal vulnerabilities, deployment credentials, customer-specific details and direct mechanisms for software supply-chain manipulation. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Collection / Supply Chain Preparation. Primary assets at risk: Private source code, Git history, Pipeline definitions, Customer code, Deployment manifests, Secrets accidentally committed. Attack-path stage: Access and Mine Source Repositories. Detection opportunities: Bulk clone/download; Search activity for secret-like strings; Rare user accessing many private repositories; Public visibility changes. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Secret scanning; Branch protection; Repository classification; Monitor mass clone/export.

data.Name: TP-05 | File and Directory Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search developer hosts, runners and build environments for credential files, SSH keys, cloud profiles, package configuration and CI/CD metadata. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer environments accumulate configuration for multiple cloud and package ecosystems. File discovery identifies exactly where secrets and tokens can be harvested. Applicability: Core / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Locate Developer Secrets and Configuration. Primary assets at risk: ~/.git-credentials, Cloud CLI profiles, npm config, SSH directories, Pipeline workspaces, Environment files. Attack-path stage: Locate Developer Secrets and Configuration. Detection opportunities: Access to known credential paths; Recursive file discovery on runner. Defensive considerations: Minimise local secrets; Ephemeral runners; Secret scanning; Credential isolation.

data.Name: TP-05 | System Owner/User Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Identify the current local user or service identity executing the compromised build or development process. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: User context helps determine which files, keys and cloud credentials are readable and whether local privilege escalation is needed. Applicability: Developer Host / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Identify Runner or Developer User. Primary assets at risk: Runner service accounts, Developer OS accounts, Build agents. Attack-path stage: Identify Runner or Developer User. Detection opportunities: whoami/id execution in runner outside expected scripts. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged runner users; No shared developer accounts.

data.Name: TP-05 | Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search developer hosts, repositories and runners for plaintext API keys, passwords, tokens, cloud profiles, package credentials and service-connection secrets. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is one of the highest-value techniques in TP-05. Decentralised CI/CD and secret-management practices increase the probability that sensitive credentials are stored in configuration files, build workspaces or project-specific tooling. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Credential Access. Primary assets at risk: Credential files, Pipeline workspace, Repository config, Cloud profiles, Package-manager config. Attack-path stage: Harvest DevOps Credentials from Files. Detection opportunities: File access to known secret paths; Secret-scanner findings; Bulk reads of environment/config files. Defensive considerations: Central secrets management; Secret scanning; Short-lived credentials; Ephemeral runners; No plaintext secrets.

data.Name: TP-05 | Unsecured Credentials: Shell History
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search shell history for credentials, tokens, registry passwords or cloud commands containing sensitive arguments. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developers and operators may accidentally paste secrets into CLI commands. Persistent self-hosted runners and admin workstations make historical command data particularly valuable. Applicability: Developer Host / Self-Hosted Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Harvest Secrets from Shell History. Primary assets at risk: bash/zsh history, PowerShell history, Developer shells. Attack-path stage: Harvest Secrets from Shell History. Detection opportunities: Unusual history-file reads; Credential scanning of shell history. Defensive considerations: Disable sensitive command logging where appropriate; Training; Ephemeral runners; Rotate exposed secrets.

data.Name: TP-05 | Credentials from Password Stores: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Retrieve build, deployment or application secrets from cloud secret-management stores such as Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Pipelines commonly fetch deployment credentials from secret stores. If the runner or DevOps identity is over-privileged, secret-store access can expose production and customer credentials. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Software supply-chain stage: Harvest CI/CD Secrets from Cloud Secret Stores. Primary assets at risk: Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Pipeline secrets. Attack-path stage: Harvest CI/CD Secrets from Cloud Secret Stores. Detection opportunities: Bulk secret retrieval; Runner/service principal accessing secrets outside expected set; Secret reads after suspicious workflow modification. Defensive considerations: Per-pipeline secret scope; Managed identities; Workload federation; PIM; Alert on bulk secret access.

data.Name: TP-05 | OS Credential Dumping: Proc Filesystem
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Read Linux process memory through /proc to recover plaintext or short-lived tokens from CI/CD runner worker processes. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Current supply-chain malware has demonstrated that ephemeral CI/CD tokens can be recovered directly from runner memory. This bypasses assumptions that short-lived tokens are safe merely because they are not stored on disk. Applicability: Linux CI/CD Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Extract Tokens from Runner Process Memory. Primary assets at risk: Runner.Worker process, OIDC tokens, GitHub tokens, Package publishing tokens. Attack-path stage: Extract Tokens from Runner Process Memory. Detection opportunities: Reads of /proc/<pid>/mem; ptrace/process-memory access by build script; Runner token used after memory-access anomaly. Defensive considerations: Isolate untrusted workflow code; Ephemeral runners; Restrict ptrace/process memory; No privileged runners.

data.Name: TP-05 | Poisoned Pipeline Execution
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Modify CI/CD workflow configuration, referenced scripts, tests, linters, build files or pull-request behavior so attacker-controlled code executes in the trusted pipeline. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the defining execution technique for TP-05. Pipeline poisoning can leak credentials, execute code on self-hosted runners, modify build output or inject malicious components that are later shipped to customers. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: CI/CD Execution. Primary assets at risk: GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Build scripts, Self-hosted runners. Attack-path stage: Poison CI/CD Pipeline. Detection opportunities: Workflow/config changes; Unexpected pull_request_target or equivalent triggers; Pipeline contacting new external endpoints; Unexpected artifact/secret export. Defensive considerations: Code review for pipeline files; No unreviewed code on privileged runners; Ephemeral isolated runners; Least-privileged pipeline identities.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: This is the defining execution technique for TP-05. Pipeline poisoning can leak credentials, execute code on self-hosted runners, modify build output or inject malicious components that are later shipped to customers. Threat-led context: MITRE documents TeamPCP and Shai-Hulud variants poisoning trusted GitHub/CI workflows. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=CI/CD Execution; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

Defensive considerations: Fine-grained tokens; API behavior monitoring; Least privilege; Workload federation.

data.Name: TP-05 | Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use shell scripts within CI/CD workflows or developer systems to execute credential theft, discovery, downloads or build modifications. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Shell execution is native to most CI/CD systems and therefore ideal for hiding malicious steps within otherwise legitimate workflows. Applicability: Linux / macOS CI/CD. Software supply-chain stage: Execute Shell Commands in Pipeline. Primary assets at risk: Linux runners, macOS runners, Build scripts, entrypoint scripts. Attack-path stage: Execute Shell Commands in Pipeline. Detection opportunities: Unexpected commands in workflow logs; New curl/wget or secret-file reads; Changes to entrypoint/setup scripts. Defensive considerations: Immutable pipeline templates; Review scripts; Ephemeral runners; Least privilege.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. data.Name: TP-05 | Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript/JScript
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use JavaScript or Node.js lifecycle scripts such as preinstall/postinstall hooks to execute malicious code during package installation or build. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Package ecosystems can automatically execute scripts. Malicious dependency or package modifications can therefore execute on developer machines and CI/CD runners simply because a trusted package is installed or built. Applicability: Node / Package Ecosystem. Software supply-chain stage: Package Execution. Primary assets at risk: npm packages, package.json scripts, Node.js build pipelines, Developer workstations. Attack-path stage: Execute JavaScript / Node Package Scripts. Detection opportunities: Unexpected install scripts; New lifecycle hooks; Package install spawning network/download processes. Defensive considerations: Disable unnecessary lifecycle scripts; Dependency pinning; Package provenance; Review package changes.

data.Name: TP-05 | Container Administration Command
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use kubectl or equivalent container administration commands to read secrets, enumerate workloads or execute actions in Kubernetes environments. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Build systems deployed on Kubernetes often have service accounts and namespace access. Excessive permissions can turn pipeline compromise into cluster compromise. Applicability: Container / Kubernetes CI/CD. Software supply-chain stage: Use Kubernetes / Container Administration. Primary assets at risk: Kubernetes, Build pods, CI namespaces, Cluster secrets. Attack-path stage: Use Kubernetes / Container Administration. Detection opportunities: kubectl get secrets; exec into unrelated workloads; Pipeline service account accessing broad namespaces. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged RBAC; Dedicated CI namespace; Short-lived service accounts; Admission controls.

data.Name: TP-05 | Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Compromise or replace software dependencies, package-manager content, development tools, IDE extensions, build plugins or CI/CD components so malicious code executes in downstream environments. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators consume large dependency ecosystems and may publish packages or use common development tools across many projects. A malicious dependency or development tool can compromise internal builds and become a route to customers. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Supply Chain Compromise. Primary assets at risk: Open-source dependencies, npm/PyPI/NuGet/Maven packages, IDE extensions, CI/CD actions/plugins, Build tools. Attack-path stage: Compromise Dependency / Development Tool. Detection opportunities: Dependency changes; New maintainers; Unexpected package version/provenance; Malicious install scripts; Integrity changes in development tools. Defensive considerations: Dependency pinning; SBOM; Package provenance/signatures; Private mirrors; Dependency review; Allow-listed CI/CD actions.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: System integrators consume large dependency ecosystems and may publish packages or use common development tools across many projects. A malicious dependency or development tool can compromise internal builds and become a route to customers. Threat-led context: MITRE v19.2 documents current attacks using compromised packages, CI/CD actions and engineering platforms. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Supply Chain Compromise; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

Defensive considerations: Reproducible builds where practical; Artifact signing; SLSA/provenance; Independent release approval; Protected build environment.

Defensive considerations: Code signing; File integrity monitoring; Immutable build images; Trusted software distribution.

data.Name: TP-05 | Software Deployment Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate software deployment, package publishing or endpoint-management tooling to distribute malicious or modified content. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators and MSPs may possess trusted deployment channels to internal or customer systems. Once CI/CD or release administration is compromised, these mechanisms can amplify the blast radius dramatically. Applicability: Core / Managed Software Delivery. Software supply-chain stage: Abuse Deployment / Release Tooling. Primary assets at risk: Deployment platforms, Release management, Package publishing, RMM/software distribution, Customer deployment tools. Attack-path stage: Abuse Deployment / Release Tooling. Detection opportunities: Mass deployment outside change window; New package/release publisher; Unexpected scripts distributed through trusted platform. Defensive considerations: Four-eyes approval; Signed packages; Change-management correlation; Separate build and deployment privilege.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: System integrators and MSPs may possess trusted deployment channels to internal or customer systems. Once CI/CD or release administration is compromised, these mechanisms can amplify the blast radius dramatically. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Core / Managed Software Delivery; SupplyChainStage=Abuse Deployment / Release Tooling; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Ingress Tool Transfer
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Download attacker tooling or second-stage payloads into a developer host, runner or build environment. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Malicious workflows commonly retrieve additional code at execution time, reducing the malicious content visible in the repository itself. Applicability: Core / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Download Additional Payload into Build / Developer Environment. Primary assets at risk: CI/CD runners, Developer hosts, Build containers. Attack-path stage: Download Additional Payload into Build / Developer Environment. Detection opportunities: curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest to new domains; Build jobs downloading unpinned binaries; Unexpected external binary transfer. Defensive considerations: Egress allow-listing for runners; Dependency proxy; Pin downloads by digest; Network monitoring.

data.Name: TP-05 | Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use sudo or cached sudo credentials to gain root-level privileges on developer or self-hosted runner systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Root access can expose other users' credentials, runner configuration, Docker sockets and persistent build-system control. Applicability: Linux / macOS Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Elevate on Developer / Runner Host. Primary assets at risk: Linux/macOS developer endpoints, Self-hosted runners, Build servers. Attack-path stage: Elevate on Developer / Runner Host. Detection opportunities: Unexpected sudo from build process; sudoers modification; Privileged commands outside pipeline baseline. Defensive considerations: No privileged runners; Dedicated build accounts; Short sudo cache; EDR.

Defensive considerations: SCIM/central lifecycle governance; Approval; Alert on admin/project account creation.

data.Description: Create or abuse an OAuth/application integration with repository, CI/CD or cloud permissions. Detection opportunities: New application/install; Admin consent; High-privilege repository scopes; App installation across many repos. Defensive considerations: App allow-listing; Admin consent workflow; Least scopes; Periodic app review.

data.Description: Create or modify a systemd service to maintain access on Linux developer or self-hosted runner systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Persistent self-hosted runners can become durable attack infrastructure inside the development network. Applicability: Linux Developer / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Persist on Linux Build / Developer Host. Primary assets at risk: Linux build servers, Self-hosted runners, Developer hosts. Attack-path stage: Persist on Linux Build / Developer Host. Detection opportunities: New systemd service; Service executable in user/temp paths. Defensive considerations: Ephemeral runners; FIM; EDR.

data.Name: TP-05 | Indicator Removal: File Deletion
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Delete temporary payloads, staging files or credential archives after use. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Short-lived CI/CD execution already creates a narrow forensic window. Explicit cleanup further reduces evidence on ephemeral or self-hosted runners. Applicability: Core / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Delete Pipeline / Credential-Theft Artifacts. Primary assets at risk: Runner workspace, /tmp, Developer filesystem. Attack-path stage: Delete Pipeline / Credential-Theft Artifacts. Detection opportunities: Rapid create-delete sequences; Deletion after external transfer; Missing workflow artifacts. Defensive considerations: Central pipeline logging; EDR on self-hosted runners; Retain runner logs externally.

data.Description: Create local archives or staging files containing collected credentials, repository data or configuration prior to exfiltration. data.Name: TP-05 | Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Code Repository
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use a code-repository service—potentially the victim's own GitHub/GitLab account—to store or exfiltrate stolen credentials and data. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Repository traffic may be trusted and allowed from developer and CI/CD systems. Attackers can exploit this trust by creating repositories or release assets that contain stolen data. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Exfiltrate Through Repository Service. Primary assets at risk: GitHub/GitLab repositories, Release assets, Stolen credentials, Source data. Attack-path stage: Exfiltrate Through Repository Service. Detection opportunities: New public repository from CI token; Unexpected release asset uploads; Runner creating repository outside approved org structure. Defensive considerations: Restrict token repo-creation rights; Monitor public repositories; DLP for code platforms.

Defensive considerations: Egress proxy; Domain allow-listing for high-trust runners; TLS inspection where appropriate.

data.Name: TP-05 | Encrypted Channel: Asymmetric Cryptography
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Encrypt collected data with attacker-controlled asymmetric keys before exfiltration. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Asymmetric encryption can ensure only the attacker can decrypt harvested CI/CD credentials, reducing the value of network/content inspection alone. Applicability: Malware / Exfiltration. Software supply-chain stage: Encrypt Stolen DevOps Data Asymmetrically. Primary assets at risk: Credential archives, Source data. Attack-path stage: Encrypt Stolen DevOps Data Asymmetrically. Detection opportunities: Encryption libraries/keys used by unexpected build process; High-entropy staged files. Defensive considerations: Behavioral monitoring; Egress controls; Ephemeral runners.

data.Name: TP-05 | Fallback Channels
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use a secondary channel such as a public repository when the primary exfiltration or command-and-control path is unavailable. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Development services are often reachable from build networks even when arbitrary internet destinations are blocked, making repository-based fallback channels attractive. Applicability: Advanced / Current Threat. Software supply-chain stage: Use Repository as Fallback Exfiltration / C2. Primary assets at risk: GitHub/GitLab, Repository APIs, CI/CD egress. Attack-path stage: Use Repository as Fallback Exfiltration / C2. Detection opportunities: Repository creation/upload following blocked external connection; Unusual API pattern from runner. Defensive considerations: Restrict repo creation; Monitor automation identities; Egress policy.

data.Name: TP-05 | Data Destruction
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Delete source clones, developer home directories, build outputs, repositories or cloud resources after compromise. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Destructive activity can disrupt development and release operations or be used as an extortion tactic. Current supply-chain malware families include wiper capabilities. Applicability: Conditional / Destructive. Software supply-chain stage: Destroy Developer / Build Data. Primary assets at risk: Developer data, Build infrastructure, Repositories, Cloud storage. Attack-path stage: Destroy Developer / Build Data. Detection opportunities: Bulk deletion; Repository deletion; Home-directory wipe; Cloud delete APIs. Defensive considerations: Immutable backups; Repository recovery; Protected backup identities; Alert on mass deletion.

Applicability=Conditional / Destructive; SupplyChainStage=Destroy Developer / Build Data; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.
